vignette:
Leilani was sixty-five years old, a widow of seven years, and a cybersecurity analyst for a regional bank. She still drove herself to the office most days, though she had stopped taking the interstate after the accident. The accident had happened two years ago, on a humid October night, when she was heading home after a late security patch rollout. A pickup truck ran a red light at the intersection of Maunaloa Avenue and forced her sedan into a spin. She remembered the smell of gasoline flooding the cabin, the way the shattered driver-side window made everything shimmer like crushed mica, and the searing pressure across her ribs as the seatbelt locked. For a few moments she could not breathe, and she was certain she would die pinned inside the wreckage. The driver of the pickup was arrested for DUI, but he received probation and a fine. Nothing else happened to him.

In the months that followed, Leilani healed physically-her ribs knitted, her left arm regained full motion-but her mind refused to let the event settle. She found herself, late at night, lying rigid in bed with her eyes fixed on the bedroom door, listening for footsteps that were not there. Sleep became a task she had to perform with vigilance; she told herself she needed to stay alert in case something came through the door. It was worse at night than during the day, and several times each week she would wake at 2 or 3 a.m. and pad through the house checking that all the locks were engaged. She had come to believe that her own body was no longer trustworthy-it had failed to protect her during the crash, and now it might fail again. What frightened her most was the sensation, when a memory returned unbidden, of the same sharp pain in her ribs, as if the metal were still bending inward. She would catch a whiff of gasoline in a parking lot and her chest would tighten, and she would see, in her mind's eye, the exact pattern of the cracked windshield. She tried to erase those images, to push the entire event out of her memory, but the harder she tried the more frequently the pictures came. She began to avoid anything that might stir emotion, positive or negative, because she had learned that joy could slide just as easily into panic.

At work, Leilana had always been valued for her steady concentration during overnight threat monitoring. Now she requested a permanent daytime shift, telling her supervisor she had trouble adjusting to the night hours. But even during the day she felt exposed. When a colleague glanced at her for too long, she felt certain they could see what had happened to her written across her face, as if the accident were a scar only she could not perceive. She started eating lunch alone in her cubicle, skipping the office birthday celebrations, declining invitations for coffee. The rumination became a loop: why had that truck hit her and not someone else? Why had she survived when the injustice of the driver's sentence had not been addressed? She would go over it and over it, searching for a meaning that never came. She had stopped watching the news because it might show a traffic report; she had stopped listening to music because a certain chord progression reminded her of the radio station playing when the crash happened. Her social circle shrank to a few phone calls with her daughter, and even those she kept short, because full conversations might lead to questions about how she was really doing.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a moment at her desk, when she froze in front of a mock phishing email because the subject line-"Your account has been compromised"-triggered the same helpless rush she had felt in the car. She could not finish the test. Her supervisor noticed and asked, kindly, if something was wrong. Leilani lied and said she had a headache, but she knew the pattern was tightening. She made an appointment with a psychologist, terrified that talking about the accident would bring the images back stronger, but also half-hoping that someone could tell her how to stop going over the same ground, how to feel safe in her own house again, and how to stop believing that everyone who looked at her already knew the whole story.
